summary: Background discussion for the Telnet proposal in RFC 137. It gives views from committee members about the arguments behind the design, to help implementers interpret and evaluate it. The authors say these are not the committee's agreed position.

plainLanguage.summary: This note explains the thinking behind the first Telnet plan. It is one member's account of the arguments, not the committee's final position, and it asks implementers to weigh the choices for themselves.

subtitle: The reasoning behind the first Telnet proposal: why a standard terminal code, why ESC, and how echo and break are handled.

tldr.problem: Implementers needed to understand why RFC 137 chose its approach to terminal handling, and to judge it before the Atlantic City meetings.
tldr.mechanism: The note sets out the arguments: one network-wide intermediate terminal code, ESC as an escape, a no-echo-from-server default with I ECHO and YOU ECHO, and X'80' with an INS to carry urgent signals.
tldr.outcome: The author calls these his understanding of the arguments, not the committee's agreed view. The note updates RFC 137, and the unit metadata lists RFC 158 as a later update.

today: RFC 139 updates RFC 137, and the unit metadata lists RFC 158 as a later update. Its status is given as Unknown.

sections.title: Why One Shared Terminal Code
sections.content:
A standard, network-wide, intermediate representation of terminal code means the using site and the serving site do not have to keep information about each other's terminals and conventions. That only works if three things hold: the serving site specifies how it maps the intermediate code to its own terminal codes, the user knows that mapping, and the using site lets the user enter all of the intermediate codes and control signals and tells the user how signals from the serving site will appear.

Other schemes were considered and rejected. A proposal that the using site translate to and from whatever code the serving site expects was rejected because every using site would need tables for every serving site, kept current as hosts were added. Because it was not known how sites would map the standard code, the user must be able to cause every one of the 128 ASCII codes.

The author stresses that these views come from various Telnet committee members and are not the agreed view of the committee.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone translates to and from one shared code, each site needs to learn only that one, instead of every other site's code. The note explains why the group chose this and rejected the alternative.

sections.title: Escape, Line Ends and Data Types
sections.content:
Serving sites are encouraged to map the full ASCII code set to their own, so that no character is left out that might later matter. Any serving-site character without a one-to-one mapping is represented by an escape string starting with ESC, also called ALT MODE. In the RFC's example, an EBCDIC site specifies that the cent sign is entered as ESC followed by C, and a using site that prints ESC as a backslash shows \C.

The network-wide end of a physical line is carriage return followed by line feed, which both sites translate as needed. A DATA TYPE byte at the start of a connection chooses the conventions in use: X'A0' for ASCII, X'A1' reserved for transparent 8-bit binary, and X'A2' reserved for EBCDIC. If the first byte has its high-order bit zero, ASCII mode is assumed. Each convention also has a way to return to control mode, and X'88' is used for that. The RFC notes that using ESC is a convention of the 7-bit ASCII mode, not a Telnet-wide standard.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer has a symbol that plain ASCII lacks, it tells the user to press the escape key and then a letter. A small first byte on each connection says which character set is in use, and one code switches back to control mode.

sections.title: Echo, Break and Urgent Signals
sections.content:
The assumed starting condition is that the using site provides any echo needed for its terminals, and the serving site gives none. This avoids trouble for sites that cannot turn their echo off or whose terminals print locally as keys are pressed. The pair I ECHO and YOU ECHO lets the two sites pass echo control between them. The RFC's example is a password prompt: the serving site asks with I ECHO, the using site agrees with YOU ECHO, the user types the password with nothing echoed, and the sites then exchange the codes again to restore the normal condition.

BREAK, or ATTN on a 2741, is sent as X'81', and reverse break as X'82'. A break can get stuck behind a full input buffer that the connection has choked off. To handle this, the user follows the special signal with an X'80'. The using site's Telnet then asks its NCP to send an INS, which warns the server to watch for the X'80'. The server treats it as a SYNC character, strips it, and returns to normal handling. If the X'80' arrives before the INS, a counting scheme keeps the behavior correct.
sections.plainLanguage: At the start, the user's own side echoes typing, and the far side does not. If a jammed line hides an urgent stop signal, the user sends a special marker and a warning note so the far side stops and looks for it.

sections.title: Minimum Implementations and Open Questions
sections.content:
A minimum using site must let the user send any chosen ASCII string, and only that string, but it may ignore and strip control signals from the serving site. A minimum serving site may map just the most important 128 serving-system controls and graphics and ignore all control signals. A site that recognizes an incoming control it cannot act on can reply with X'87' followed by the code it received.

Whenever an ASCII Telnet connection is lost, the other end should assume that the process was quit, aborted or failed. The note also asks an open question: should a protocol such as Telnet add functions that go beyond a local system's own capacity, such as hold output or kill print, and if so, to what extent should those be network-wide standards rather than local choices. It calls for a mechanism to assign and announce DATA TYPE and control codes.

The endnotes correct RFC 137: drop a stray letter in one word, treat X'85' as Reserved, answer a received X'88' with a double X'88' when the new data type can be handled, and assume the using site echoes if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: A small, simple implementation may ignore the advanced signals, and a lost connection means the other side assumes the session ended. The note ends by asking whether Telnet should offer extras that a local system does not have.
